facts.statement: Caririsuchus lived during the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Cretaceous

facts.statement: Caririsuchus inhabited the Romualdo Formation in the Araripe Basin of northeastern Brazil during the Aptian to Albian stages.
facts.quote: Caririsuchus is an extinct genus of itasuchid crocodylomorph from the Aptian to Albian Romualdo Formation of the Santana Group in the Araripe Basin in northeastern Brazil.

facts.statement: The more complete fossil slab from which the type material was taken was illegally shipped to Europe and is now believed to be in a private collection with unknown current whereabouts.
facts.quote: but the much more complete fossil slab that these pieces were taken from was illegally shipped to Europe before being presumably sold into a private collection with its current whereabouts unknown.

facts.statement: Some of the Caririsuchus remains that remained in Brazil were destroyed in a 2018 fire at the Rio de Janeiro fossil collection.
facts.quote: Some of the few remains that had stayed in Brazil were destroyed in the 2018 fire that destroyed large parts of the collection held in Rio de Janeiro.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus is classified as a member of the clade Notosuchia, typically placed in the clade Itasuchidae alongside relatives like Pepesuchus and Itasuchus.
facts.quote: The genus is considered to be a member of the clade Notosuchia, usually as a close relative to other platyrostral forms like Pepesuchus and Itasuchus in the clade Itasuchidae

facts.statement: Some authors debate the classification of Caririsuchus, placing it in the peirosaurid subfamily Pepesuchinae instead of Itasuchidae.
facts.quote: though some authors have placed all these forms in the peirosaurid subfamily Pepesuchinae.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus was a semi-aquatic animal that lived in the coastal environment of the Romualdo Formation.
facts.quote: Caririsuchus was a semi-aquatic animal that once inhabited the coastal Romualdo Formation.

facts.statement: Brazilian paleontologist Alexander Kellner described the new genus and species Caririsuchus camposi in 1987.
facts.quote: Brazilian paleontologist Alexander Kellner was able to determine that the animal represented a new species and genus, which he described in 1987 as Caririsuchus camposi.

facts.statement: The genus name Caririsuchus honors the Kiriri people who historically inhabited the Araripe Basin in Brazil.
facts.quote: Caririsuchus was named for the Kiriri people who once inhabited large parts of Brazil including the Araripe Basin.

facts.statement: The species name camposi was chosen to honor Brazilian paleontologist and geologist Diogenes de Almeida Campos.
facts.quote: The species name on the other hand was chosen to honor Diogenes de Almeida Campos, a Brazilian paleontologist and geologist noted for his contribution to the study of the Araripe Basin.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus possessed a high triangular skull with a moderately laterally compressed, tapering, flattened snout that widened toward the back of the skull.
facts.quote: Caririsuchus had a comparably high triangular skull with a moderately laterally-compressed, tapering platyrostral (flattened) snout that gradually widens towards the back of the skull.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus had large, circular eyesockets that were directed more laterally.
facts.quote: The eyesockets are large, circular and directed more laterally.

facts.statement: Like the upper jaw, the mandible of Caririsuchus exhibited a festooned toothrow forming two waves upon which the teeth were placed.
facts.quote: Like the upper jaw the mandible exhibits a festooned toothrow forming two waves that the teeth are placed atop of.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Caririsuchus likely held between 21 and 22 teeth, with four located in the premaxilla and the rest in the maxilla.
facts.quote: The upper jaw of Caririsuchus is thought to contain 21 or 22 teeth, four of which in the premaxilla and the remainder in the maxilla.

facts.statement: All teeth of Caririsuchus possessed finely serrated edges, with front teeth being pointed and rear teeth being smaller, blunter, and more compressed.
facts.quote: All teeth have finely serrated edges and the anterior teeth are generally more pointed whereas the teeth in the back of the jaw are smaller, blunter, more uniform and more labiolingually compressed.

facts.statement: Research suggests Caririsuchus teeth were closely spaced and arranged in an overbite rather than interlocking, similar to modern alligators.
facts.quote: Pinheiro and colleagues note that the teeth of Caririsuchus were closely spaced and that the skull shows no clearly visible occlusal scars, which would suggest that like modern alligators the teeth of this taxon didn't interlock but instead were arranged in an overbite.

facts.statement: Alexander Kellner noted that the femur of Caririsuchus was 25% larger than its humerus.
facts.quote: Alexander Kellner describes the femur as being 25% larger than the humerus.

facts.statement: Eric Buffetaut described Caririsuchus as one of the most heavily armored crocodilians known.
facts.quote: Caririsuchus has been repeatedly noted for its extensive osteoderm armor, with Eric Buffetaut calling it "one of the most heavily armored of all known crocodilians".

facts.statement: Caririsuchus armor extended from just behind the head to the tail tip, featuring a single double row running along the neck and torso.
facts.quote: The armor stretches from just behind the head to the tip of the tail and is composed of a single parasagittal double row across the neck and torso.

facts.statement: Individual osteoderms on Caririsuchus were rectangular, wider than long, and increased in size from the head to the mid-body before shrinking toward the hips.
facts.quote: The individual plates are rectangular, wider than long and grow larger from the head to the middle of the body before decreasing in size towards the hip.

facts.statement: The midline osteoderms of Caririsuchus overlapped but lacked the articulation processes found at the anterolateral corners of some other crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: The parasagittal osteoderms are noted as overlapping each other but lacking articulation processes at their anterolateral corner as in some other crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus osteoderms featured low, wide midline keels and ornamentation of pits radiating outward from the center of each scute.
facts.quote: They are further described as possessing low and wide keels down their midline and an ornamentation consisting of a pattern of pits that seems to radiate outward from the center of each scute.

facts.statement: Eric Buffetaut noted that Caririsuchus possessed ventral armor protecting the stomach and that its limbs were also covered in bony scutes.
facts.quote: The presence of ventral armor protecting the stomach is mentioned by Buffetaut, who furthermore notes that the limbs were similarly covered by bony scutes.

facts.statement: Based on the holotype, Caririsuchus was a small animal measuring 1.5 meters from snout to tail tip.
facts.quote: Based on the holotype specimen Caririsuchus was a relatively small animal, only measuring 1.5 m in length from the tip of the snout to the end of the tail.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus is interpreted as a semi-aquatic animal based on its broad snout.
facts.quote: Caririsuchus with its platyrostral snout has been interpreted as a semi-aquatic animal.

facts.statement: Eric Buffetaut was the first to classify Caririsuchus in the family Trematochampsidae, treating it as a species of Itasuchus.
facts.quote: The first person to place the taxon in a specific family was Eric Buffetaut, who regarded the animal to simply be another species of Itasuchus and therefore placed it in the family Trematochampsidae.

facts.statement: In 2018, Geroto and Bertini established the subfamily Pepesuchinae within Peirosauridae, including Caririsuchus as a distinct genus alongside Itasuchus, Pepesuchus, and Barreirosuchus.
facts.quote: Geroto and Bertini established the clade Pepesuchinae in 2018 as a subfamily of Peirosauridae, initially consisting of Caririsuchus (treated as a distinct genus from Itasuchus), Itasuchus, Pepesuchus and Barreirosuchus.

facts.statement: The validity of the family Trematochampsidae is debated, with its type genus considered dubious and its members now distributed among various groups within Notosuchia.
facts.quote: Since then, studies have cast doubt over the validity of Trematochampsidae as a family, with the type genus being regarded as dubious and chimeric while its members have been divided among several different groups within Notosuchia.

facts.statement: A polytomy among Caririsuchus, Itasuchus, Pepesuchus, and Roxochampsa has led to debate over whether all four should be merged into the genus Itasuchus.
facts.quote: In this work all four taxa were recovered in a polytomy, leading to a brief discussion of whether or not all four taxa should be placed in the genus Itasuchus as had been done by Buffetaut for Caririsuchus camposi.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus fossils are found only in the Romualdo Formation in Brazil's Araripe Basin.
facts.quote: The fossils of Caririsuchus are exclusively known from the Romualdo Formation (Santana Group), a Konservat-Lagerstätte located in Brazil′s Araripe Basin.

facts.statement: The habitat of Caririsuchus likely included lagoons, deltas, and possibly an inland sea.
facts.quote: Overall the paleoenvironment may have featured a variety of near-shore environments, with interpretations suggesting the presence of lagoons, deltas and even an inland sea.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus lived in a tropical climate that was warm and ranged from semiarid to arid.
facts.quote: The palynoflora of the Romualdo Formation is typical of a tropical setting with a warm paleoclimate and semiarid to arid conditions.

facts.statement: Fossils of Caririsuchus are well preserved because the ancient seafloor had low oxygen levels.
facts.quote: The Romualdo Formation is well known for its excellent preservation of vertebrates due to the low oxygen conditions likely present at the seafloor.

facts.statement: Caririsuchus belongs to the subfamily Pepesuchinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Pepesuchinae

facts.statement: Caririsuchus is classified within the family Peirosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Peirosauridae

facts.statement: Caririsuchus lived during the Aptian stage, between 119.57 and 113.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (119.57 to 113.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Caririsuchus has been recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 1
